title: Checkpoint: Mammals
objective: After this level you can compare the main groups of mammals and how they live.
summary: Mammals start life three ways: monotremes lay eggs, marsupials finish in a pouch, placentals grow in the womb fed by a placenta. Elephants carry young up to about 22 months.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: three ways to start a mammal's life.
cards.body: Every mammal in this chapter feeds its young milk. But they don't all begin the same way. Line up an echidna, a kangaroo and an elephant, and you're looking at an egg, a pouch and the longest pregnancy of any mammal.

items.label: Monotreme: echidna
points: Suckles in the pouch until prickly

cards.headline: The placenta's trick
cards.body: In placental mammals, an organ called the placenta passes nutrients and wastes between the mother's blood and her unborn baby's. So the young can grow for a long time and be born well developed: an elephant carries her calf up to about 22 months, longer than any other mammal. Placentals are every living mammal except marsupials and monotremes: the lion, whale, bat, chimp and dog in this chapter, and you.

mascot.line: Egg, pouch or placenta: three routes, one destination. Milk.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: What makes a mammal a mammal, and how mammals start life as eggs, in pouches or in the womb.
How whales and dolphins pass the mammal checklist while living their whole lives at sea.
How bats fly on wings made from hands and find their food by listening to echoes.
Why chimps are our cousins, not our ancestors, and dogs came from ancient wolves, not today's.

questions.prompt: Mammals recap: what does a placenta do?

options.label: Passes nutrients and wastes between mother and baby
Keeps an egg warm
options.rationale: That's a monotreme job, and no placenta is involved.

questions.explanation: The placenta passes nutrients and wastes between the mother's blood and her unborn baby's.

questions.prompt: Mammals recap: a newborn elephant is far more developed than a newborn kangaroo. Why?

options.label: It grows in the womb up to about 22 months, fed by a placenta
Kangaroos skip the milk stage
options.rationale: Joeys suckle for about a year.

options.label: Elephant calves hatch in a pouch

questions.explanation: A placenta lets the elephant calf grow in the womb for up to about 22 months; a kangaroo is born after about 33 days.

questions.prompt: Mammals recap: which of this chapter's animals is NOT a placental mammal?
questions.explanation: Echidnas are monotremes; placentals are every living mammal except marsupials and monotremes.

questions.prompt: Mammals recap, from Level 15: how does a bat use echolocation?

options.label: It listens for echoes of its own calls
It follows the smell of insects
It sees heat in the dark
It copies other bats' flight paths
options.rationale: Each bat reads its own echoes.

questions.explanation: A bat sends out calls, mostly ultrasound, and the echoes that return tell it what's around.

questions.prompt: Mammals recap, from Level 13: in the Amboseli study, what made some elephant families better at spotting strangers?

options.label: A larger herd
options.rationale: The key was the leader's age.

options.label: A strong adult male
options.rationale: Adult males roam apart from the herd.

options.label: A longer trunk
options.rationale: The difference was in the leader.

questions.explanation: Families led by matriarchs aged 55 or more told strangers' calls from familiar ones far better.
